questions.question: What are classes and objects in Ruby?
questions.title: Classes and Objects
questions.direct_answer: A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance. `class Dog; def bark; 'Woof'; end; end; d = Dog.new; d.bark` -> 'Woof'. `new` calls `initialize` (the constructor), which sets up instance variables (@name): `def initialize(name); @name = name; end`. Instance variables (@x) hold per-object state; instance methods define behavior. `Dog.new('Rex')` creates an object of class Dog; `d.class` is Dog; `d.is_a?(Dog)` is true. Classes are objects too (Class) — Dog is an instance of Class, so classes have methods (Dog.new, Dog.name). Inheritance: class Puppy < Dog; end (Puppy gets Dog's methods). Everything in Ruby is an object (numbers, strings, nil, classes) — they all have methods and a class. Define a class with state (initialize + @vars) and behavior (methods); create instances with new.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know a class is a blueprint, an object is an instance, new calls initialize, and @vars hold state.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting to set @vars in initialize (nil later), or confusing class (Dog) with instance (d).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Class = blueprint; object = instance (Dog.new). new calls initialize; @vars = per-object state. Everything is an object. Inheritance: Puppy < Dog.

sections.title: Classes + Objects
sections.content:
class = blueprint; object = instance (Dog.new). new -> initialize; @vars = state. Everything is an object.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C[class Dog] --> N[Dog.new('Rex')]
  N --> I[initialize sets @name]
  N --> M[d.bark uses @name]
  P[Puppy < Dog] --> Inh[inherits Dog's methods]
```

sections.title: Classes and objects
sections.content:
```ruby
# A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance
class Dog
  def initialize(name); @name = name; end   # constructor (new calls this)
  def bark;        "#{@name} says Woof"; end   # instance method
end

d = Dog.new('Rex')      # new -> initialize -> @name = 'Rex'
d.bark                  # 'Rex says Woof'
d.class                 # Dog
d.is_a?(Dog)           # true

# Instance variables = per-object STATE; instance methods = BEHAVIOR
class Counter
  def initialize; @n = 0; end
  def inc; @n += 1; end
  def count; @n; end
end
c = Counter.new
c.inc; c.inc; c.count   # 2  (state lives on the instance)

# Everything is an object (numbers, strings, nil, even classes):
42.class                # Integer
'hi'.class             # String
nil.class              # NilClass
Dog.class              # Class   (classes are objects of Class)

# Inheritance: subclass gets superclass's methods
class Puppy < Dog
  def yap; 'yip'; end
end
p = Puppy.new('Buddy')
p.bark                 # 'Buddy says Woof' (inherited from Dog)
p.yap                  # 'yip'
p.is_a?(Dog)          # true
p.is_a?(Puppy)        # true

# Define STATE (initialize + @vars) + BEHAVIOR (methods); create with new.
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Forgetting to set @vars in initialize (they're nil later).
Confusing the class (Dog) with an instance (d) — Dog is the blueprint, d is one object.
Forgetting everything is an object (even nil and classes).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance (Dog.new creates one).
`new` calls `initialize` (the constructor), which sets instance variables (@name).
Instance variables (@x) hold per-object state; instance methods define behavior.
Classes are objects too (Dog is an instance of Class); everything is an object.
Inheritance: class Puppy < Dog; end — Puppy gets Dog's methods.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance. class Dog; def bark; Woof; end; end; d Dog dot new; d dot bark to Woof. new calls initialize (the constructor), which sets up instance variables (name): def initialize name; name var name; end. Instance variables (x) hold per-object state; instance methods define behavior. Dog new Rex creates an object of class Dog; d dot class is Dog; d dot is_a Dog is true. Classes are objects too (Class) — Dog is an instance of Class, so classes have methods (Dog dot new, Dog dot name). Inheritance: class Puppy less-than Dog; end (Puppy gets Dog's methods). Everything in Ruby is an object (numbers, strings, nil, classes) — they all have methods and a class. Define a class with state (initialize plus vars) and behavior (methods); create instances with new. A common mistake is forgetting to set vars in initialize, leaving them nil, and confusing the class with an instance.
